newsitem.title: FINLAND: FEATURE - Finns chart path from isolation to integration.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Finns chart path from isolation to integration.

text.p: First-timers here for the Clinton-Yeltsin summit may be in for a few surprises. There will be daylight. People will not run about brandishing knives or birch twigs. They will talk a lot -- albeit on mobile phones.

Not that visitors can expect to understand much: the Finnish language sounds completely alien to Indo-European ears. As an illustration, sounds like "yaw", "niin", "on", and "totta kai" mean people are agreeing with each other. "Kylla" means yes.

Strangeness, isolation and its proximity to Russia have for years kept much of Finland in a cultural and political grey zone in the minds of many outsiders. The complexity of its relations with both East and West has fuelled misunderstanding.

A member of the European Union since 1995, political Finland was for much of the post-war period locked in a degree of suspicion or ignorance as it sought to co-exist as a Western state with the former Soviet Union to its east.

"In Hollywood lore, Finland is used as a point of reference for something really remote, a strange location of which no one knows practically anything," writes journalist Jouni Hokkanen in 'City', a freesheet guide.
In British writers' hands, he adds, "Finland seems to equal sauna, 'puukko' the knife, 'Koskenkorva' the vodka, incomprehensible language and the Winter War".

That is a view partly cultivated by the Finns themselves avoiding questions about the 70s and 80s when, for instance, the Finnish edition of Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn's "Gulag Archipelago" had to be published in Sweden.
But when Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin meet here on March 20, they will see a city full of colour and life.

And among themselves, their Finnish hosts are now breaking Cold War taboos: examining the self-censorship which spawned the term "Finlandisation" and debating whether Finland, too, should join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).

"Finland has turned its foreign policy 180 degrees, from East to West," said Janne Virkkunen, editor-in-chief of the leading daily, Helsingin Sanomat. "It has happened in such a short time. It started in 1989."
TWO WARS AGAINST THE SOVIET UNION

Finland, "Suomi" to the five million Finns, will be 80 this December 6 when it celebrates its declaration of independence. A former Grand Duchy of Russia and before that part of Sweden, this relatively young nation is vigorously patriotic.

Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin has been portrayed as bestowing independence to Finland in 1917 after hiding out here planning his revolution. But the Finns' resistance to communism was so great it sparked civil war, which the Reds lost.

For many Finns, the subsequent "Winter War" referred to by the freesheet is a defining moment in the history of their republic: in the run-up to World War Two, a secret pact between the Kremlin and Nazi Germany put Finland in the Soviet sphere.
Seeking territory to secure the strategic position of Leningrad, but perceiving Finland as unable to resist Nazi encroachment, the Soviet Union attacked in 1939.

The tale of how the vastly outnumbered Finns fought alone with guts, guile and white camouflage, in snow-swept forests through one of the coldest winters ever, and defeated the vast but ill-prepared Red Army, shows the stuff Finns are made of.
A total of 1.5 million Red Army soldiers were sent to Finland to fight against about a quarter of a million Finns.

Soviet dictator Josef Stalin, on record as finding the Finns "a remarkably slow-witted people" who needed "to be hit over the head with the sledgehammer of common sense", later said: "the Finns have only their skis left -- but their supply of skis never runs out".

The Winter War is credited with the invention of the Molotov Cocktail -- bottles filled with kerosene, tar and gasoline sealed loosely with a rag, set alight and hurled under or into Red Army tanks, and named after Soviet foreign minister Vyacheslav Molotov.
It has also spawned a much-quoted military joke: there are possibly a million Russian soldiers in Finland, and all are welcome to stay where they belong -- underground.

Even though the Finns repelled Soviet forces, to settle in 1940 they had to give up one-tenth of Finland. This sowed the seeds of renewed conflict and in 1941 Finland supported a German attack on the Soviet Union, starting the Continuation War.
By aligning themselves with the Germans -- in the eyes of the Finnish leadership the lesser of two mighty evils -- the Finns forced a reluctant Britain to declare war on them.

The Continuation War settlement, as World War Two was entering its final stages, left Finland with no territory regained, heavy war reparations to pay to Moscow, and -- until 1947 -- under a Soviet-led Allied Control Commission.
COLD WAR ISOLATION
With the onset of the Cold War Helsinki, remaining independent and capitalist but needing to repay war debts, built up barter trade with the Soviet Union.
Moscow, ostensibly nervous of attack from the West, sought a Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with Finland not unlike those it sealed with Eastern European nations.

The Finns resisted: a final treaty in 1948 committed them to repel an armed attack by Germany or its allies on or through Finland, and to Soviet help in defence "subject to mutual agreement". That was renewed until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Finland in the 1970s and 80s maintained close ties with the Kremlin and in Western eyes lingered in a grey zone, prompting an Austrian politician to warn of "Finlandisation", or creeping Sovietisation.
"The Finns have always been on the side of the West, they just couldn't always say it," said one Western diplomat: a view many Finnish politicians are now happy to foster.

Tensions with Moscow ebbed and flowed with the forces of detente and disarmament, and as Finland tried to face both east and west in increasing secrecy to avoid kindling Soviet wrath, public debate became increasingly muted.
"The problem of the 70s comes out of the fact that the younger generation of Finnish politicians then...started to believe the Soviet propaganda," said Virkkunen.
JOINING THE WESTERN CLUB

In his view, the 1989 turning point in Finnish foreign policy came with its scrambling accession to the Council of Europe, just two weeks before Hungary: a move long resisted by the then president Mauno Koivisto.

Finns deny that the Soviet Union's collapse "freed" them to enter the then European Community: Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen last year said he had been discussing the possibility of membership in Moscow in 1990, and met no resistance.

But many do see membership of the Union -- approved by 57 percent of the population in a 1994 referendum -- as a cornerstone of the country's security and a sign they are at last "in the club" of Western nations.
"My kids can't even understand communism, that the Soviet Union was a superpower threatening Finland," said Virkkunen.
